definition: Visual explanations highlighting which input regions most influenced a prediction, via gradients or activation maps.
details: Visual explanations highlighting which input regions most influenced a prediction, via gradients or activation maps. Intuitive for images and spectrograms; known to sometimes look convincing while being unfaithful, so treat as hypothesis, not proof.

explainer.lead: Saliency maps show which parts of an input most influenced a prediction, making model behaviour easier to inspect. They matter because they offer an intuitive visual check on image and spectrogram models, though a convincing map is not proof of faithfulness.

tiers.eli5: Like a heat-shaded overlay on a photo showing which spots the model was looking at when it made its call.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers compute them from gradients or activation maps to sanity-check what an image or audio model attends to. The pitfall is trusting a plausible-looking map as evidence of the model's real reasoning.
tiers.paperLevel: Regions are scored by the magnitude of the gradient of the output with respect to input pixels, or by activation maps, and highlighted. A known limit: maps can appear convincing while being unfaithful to the actual decision.

explainer.example: For a spectrogram classified as a dog bark, the saliency map highlights the frequency bands the model weighted most.
